blocks.text: Of all the comparisons in this module, MCP versus function calling is the one people mix up most, because the two are not actually competitors, they are two different halves of the exact same overall process. Function calling is about what a model outputs when it decides to use a tool, MCP is about what happens once that output reaches the other side of the connection. This lesson makes that boundary precise.
1. What Function Calling Actually Means

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A model chooses a function and arguments

blocks.text: Function calling, sometimes called tool calling depending on the vendor, is a capability built into a model itself, the model is trained to recognize when a task needs an external action, and to output a structured, well-formed request for that action, a function name and a set of arguments, instead of a plain text answer.

code.content:
# a rough example of a model's own function-calling output
{"function_call": {"name": "get_weather", "arguments": "{\"city\": \"Mumbai\"}"}}

blocks.title: A useful way to think about it
blocks.content: Function calling is the model deciding and describing what it wants, in its own words and format, nothing about that decision involves MCP at all.

blocks.text: This capability is trained into the model during its own training process, it is not something a developer configures after the fact, a developer only supplies the list of available function descriptions for a given request.

blocks.title: Terminology note
blocks.content: Some vendors call this feature tool use, others call it function calling, others tool calling, they all refer to essentially the same underlying capability.

blocks.text: 2. What MCP Actually Means, Restated

MCP, as covered throughout this module, is the standard for how a client discovers what tools exist and how it actually delivers a call to a server and gets a result back. MCP does not decide when a model wants to call a tool, that decision, and the exact output shape of the request, is function calling’s job.

It can help to think of MCP as starting exactly where function calling ends, the moment a model has expressed an intention, MCP takes over to make that intention actually happen against a real system.

code.content:
# MCP knows nothing about how the model decided to call this
mcp_client.call_tool("get_weather", {"city": "Mumbai"})   # this line is identical regardless of which model asked for it

blocks.text: This is exactly why MCP servers are so easily reused across projects that use completely different AI models, the server has no concept of function calling at all, it only ever sees standard MCP requests.
3. Where the Two Actually Meet

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Function calling and MCP meet at a common point

blocks.text: In a real system, the model uses its own function-calling format to express "I want to call get_weather with city Mumbai." The host application takes that expressed intention and translates it into an actual MCP tools/call request sent to the appropriate server. The model never speaks MCP directly, and an MCP server never sees the model’s native function-calling format directly, the host sits in between, translating one into the other.

code.content:
# the host is the translation point, never the model, never the server directly
model_intention = model.function_call   # provider specific
mcp_request = translate_to_mcp(model_intention)   # host does this
mcp_response = mcp_client.send(mcp_request)

blocks.text: If the host’s translation logic has a bug, the symptoms usually show up as a tool call that seems to vanish or fail silently, even though both the model’s intention and the MCP server itself were working correctly.
4. Function Calling Without MCP

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A model calls a hardcoded function

blocks.text: It is entirely possible to use function calling without MCP at all, a developer can define a function schema directly in whatever format their specific model provider expects, and write custom code that executes that function when the model requests it. This works fine for a single application talking to a single model, but it reintroduces the exact M times N integration problem MCP was built to solve the moment more than one tool or more than one application is involved.

This is a completely reasonable choice for a small, single-purpose project, the cost only becomes apparent once a second tool, or a second application, needs the exact same integration rebuilt from scratch.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","Reuse across a second application"],"rows":[["Direct, hand-rolled function calling","Requires rebuilding the same glue code"],["Function calling plus MCP","The MCP server is reused as-is"]]}

blocks.text: This is a completely legitimate starting point for a quick prototype, plenty of production systems began exactly this way before growing into a more standardized MCP-based setup once reuse needs appeared.
5. MCP Without Function Calling

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: An MCP server can be manually invoked with no model involved

blocks.text: It is also possible, in principle, for a system to use MCP servers without relying on a model’s native function-calling capability at all, for instance, a rule-based or scripted application could call MCP tools directly based on fixed logic, with no AI model deciding anything. This is uncommon in practice, but it illustrates that MCP itself is not intrinsically tied to AI models, it is just a general tool-discovery-and-invocation protocol.

This scenario is rare in practice specifically because the whole point of most MCP deployments is enabling an AI model to decide dynamically what to call, but it is a useful reminder that MCP itself has no built-in dependency on any specific AI capability.
6. Why Function-Calling Formats Differ Between Providers

Different model providers trained their models on slightly different function-calling conventions, one might expect arguments as a JSON string, another as a native object, one might support parallel tool calls in a single turn, another might not. This variation is exactly why a tool integration built directly against one provider’s function-calling format does not automatically work with a different provider’s model.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Layer","Where variation exists","Standardized by"],"rows":[["Function calling output","Differs by model provider","Not standardized, provider-specific"],["Tool description and invocation on the server side","The same regardless of model","MCP"]]}
{"headers":["Provider convention","Arguments format"],"rows":[["Convention A","Arguments as a JSON encoded string"],["Convention B","Arguments as a native structured object"]]}

blocks.text: This divergence is not a mistake on anyone’s part, different research teams simply made different reasonable design choices, the divergence is exactly the kind of thing a shared protocol on the tool side can insulate a system from.
A host application built to support multiple model providers typically maintains a small adapter per provider specifically to normalize these differences before anything reaches the MCP layer.
7. The Host Application Bridges the Two

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: A function-calling format bridges through the host application to the MCP protocol

blocks.text: The host application, introduced in the MCP Architecture lesson, is exactly where this translation logic lives, it receives the model’s function-call output in whatever provider-specific shape it takes, maps it to the correct MCP client and tool name, sends the MCP request, and then translates the MCP result back into whatever format the model expects to see next.

code.content:
# a simplified translation step inside a host application
model_call = model.get_function_call()   # provider-specific shape
result = mcp_clients[model_call.tool_name].call_tool(model_call.tool_name, model_call.arguments)
model.provide_tool_result(result)         # translated back for the model to continue reasoning

blocks.text: Most modern MCP client SDKs include helper utilities specifically for this translation step, reducing how much of this bridging code a host application developer needs to write by hand.

blocks.title: A helpful way to picture this
blocks.content: The host is a bit like an interpreter at a meeting between two people who speak different languages, the model on one side, the MCP server on the other, translating fluently between them.

blocks.text: Well-tested translation logic in the host is arguably one of the most underappreciated pieces of a reliable AI application, small mismatches here are a common source of subtle, hard-to-reproduce bugs.
8. Why This Split Is Actually a Feature

Keeping function calling and MCP as two separate layers, rather than one combined system, is exactly what gives a team the freedom to swap models without rewriting their tools, and to add new tools without needing the model provider’s permission or involvement at all. Each side can evolve independently.

Contrast this with a hypothetical world where tool integration logic was baked directly into a specific model provider’s SDK, switching providers in that world would mean rewriting every single tool from scratch.

blocks.title: The core payoff restated
blocks.content: Two independently replaceable pieces beat one tightly fused piece, whenever either half is likely to change on its own schedule, and models and tools very much do.

blocks.text: It also means a bug fix to a tool can ship immediately to every connected model, past, present, or future, without waiting on any model provider release cycle at all.
9. What Happens When a Model Supports No Native Function Calling

Some models, particularly smaller or older ones, do not support structured function calling at all, in these cases a host application sometimes falls back to asking the model to output tool calls as plain text in a specific format, then parsing that text manually, this is less reliable than native function calling but still ultimately connects to the exact same MCP layer underneath.

code.content:
# a text-based fallback for a model without native function calling
text_output = model.generate(prompt)
if "CALL_TOOL:" in text_output:
    tool_name, args = parse_tool_call_text(text_output)
    mcp_client.call_tool(tool_name, args)

blocks.text: This text-parsing fallback is inherently less reliable than native function calling, since it depends on the model consistently formatting its intention in exactly the expected way, but it still lets even an older or smaller model participate in an MCP-based system.
Some teams intentionally choose this text-based approach even for models that do support native function calling, when they need a capability the native format does not yet expose.
10. Parallel and Sequential Tool Calls

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Parallel calls are compared against sequential calls

blocks.text: Some models can request several function calls in a single turn, intending them to run in parallel, MCP itself does not dictate whether calls happen in parallel or one after another, that orchestration decision is made by the host, which might call several MCP servers concurrently or in sequence depending on what makes sense for the task.

A host might choose to run two independent MCP tool calls concurrently to save time, while running two dependent calls, where the second needs the first’s result, strictly in sequence, this scheduling decision lives entirely in the host, not in MCP itself.

A host might also impose its own safety limits here, capping how many tool calls can run in parallel, or requiring certain high-risk tools to always run one at a time with explicit confirmation between them.

This is another reason the host layer matters so much in practice, it carries real responsibility for orchestration decisions that neither the model nor the MCP server are positioned to make on their own.
11. A Common Point of Confusion

People sometimes ask "should I use MCP or function calling," as if forced to choose one, but the honest answer is that in any real AI application capable of taking action, both are present, function calling to know when and what the model wants to do, MCP to standardize what actually happens once that intention needs to be carried out.

blocks.title: A one-line answer worth memorizing
blocks.content: Function calling: what the model wants. MCP: how that want actually gets carried out.

blocks.text: This confusion is understandable, both concepts are usually introduced together in tutorials and documentation, since a working system genuinely needs both, but they solve different problems and evolve on different timelines.
12. Testing These Two Layers Separately

Because function calling and MCP are separate layers, they can, and should, be tested somewhat independently, testing whether a model reliably decides to call the right tool at the right time is a model-behavior question, testing whether a tool call actually executes correctly and returns a sensible result is an MCP-server question.

code.content:
# testing the MCP layer alone, no model involved
result = mcp_client.call_tool("get_weather", {"city": "Mumbai"})
assert "temperature_c" in result

blocks.text: Separating these tests also makes it much clearer where to look first when a bug report comes in, did the model ask for the wrong thing, or did the right request fail somewhere along the way.
13. Switching Models Without Touching Your Tools

blocks.title: Diagram summary
blocks.content: Model A and model B share the same tools

blocks.text: This split is precisely what makes it possible to swap in a new model release and keep every existing MCP server exactly as it is, the host layer’s translation code might need a small update to handle the new model’s function-calling format, but the tools themselves, and the servers behind them, do not change at all.
Teams that have gone through a real model migration consistently point to this as one of the most concrete, tangible benefits of having kept these two layers cleanly separated from the start.

code.content:
# only this adapter layer changes when switching providers
adapter = ADAPTERS[current_model_provider]
mcp_request = adapter.translate(model_output)

blocks.text: 14. A Worked Example: Tracing One Full Round Trip

A user asks "what is the weather in Delhi." The model uses its own function-calling format to output an intention to call get_weather with city Delhi. The host translates this into an MCP tools/call request against the weather server. The server returns a result in the standard MCP result shape. The host translates that result back into whatever format the model expects, and the model uses it to produce a final natural-language answer.

code.content:
intention = model.function_call        # provider format
mcp_result = mcp_client.call_tool("get_weather", {"city": "Delhi"})   # MCP format
final_answer = model.continue_with_tool_result(mcp_result)            # back to provider format

blocks.text: Notice that if this same user had been talking to a different model provider, only the very first translation step would look different, everything from the MCP request onward stays exactly the same.

code.content:
# the same round trip, now against a second model provider
intention_b = model_b.function_call        # different shape than model_a
mcp_result = mcp_client.call_tool("get_weather", {"city": "Delhi"})   # identical either way

blocks.text: 15. Common Mistakes When Comparing the Two

items: Treating MCP and function calling as competing alternatives rather than two complementary layers.
Assuming MCP standardizes the model’s own output format, it does not, that remains provider-specific.
Assuming function calling alone solves the reuse and discoverability problems MCP was built for, it only solves the "what does the model want to do" half.
Forgetting the host application is doing real translation work between the two, and needs to be built or configured correctly for the whole system to function.

blocks.text: A fifth common mistake is assuming a more capable model reduces the need for a well-designed MCP server, a smarter model still depends entirely on the tools available to it actually working correctly and being described clearly.
A sixth common mistake is assuming a model provider’s function-calling documentation is also documentation for MCP, they describe two entirely separate specifications maintained by different parties.
16. Practice: Trace Your Own Round Trip

Pick any AI application idea involving a single tool call, and write out, step by step, exactly what format the model’s output would take, what the host would need to translate it into for MCP, and what the MCP result would look like coming back.

code.content:
steps = [
    "1. Model outputs a function call in its own format",
    "2. Host maps that to an MCP tools/call request",
    "3. MCP server executes and returns a standard result",
    "4. Host translates the result back for the model",
]
for s in steps: print(s)

blocks.text: Once you have traced through one round trip, try imagining the same scenario with a model that has no native function-calling support at all, and note where the text-parsing fallback from earlier in this lesson would need to slot in.
Compare your traced steps against the worked example earlier in this lesson, and see if you can spot exactly which step would need to change if you swapped in a different model provider.
Key Takeaway

Function calling and MCP are not rivals, function calling is how a model expresses what it wants to do, in whatever format its provider trained it to use, MCP is the standardized layer that turns that expressed intention into an actual, reliable call against a real tool, resource, or prompt, and turns the result back into something the model can use.

This lesson closes the Introduction to MCP module. With the motivation, problems solved, architecture, workflow, terminology, ecosystem, and every major comparison now covered at an introductory level, the next module, MCP Fundamentals, goes one level deeper into each core concept, starting with the client.

The testing-separately point from the newly added section is worth carrying forward, when something goes wrong in a real system, the fastest way to debug it is asking which of the two layers actually failed, the model’s decision, or the MCP call that carried it out.
